paragraphs: Distributed optimization divides learning work across machines, but those machines still need to exchange information. This paper studies how to reduce that communication while solving a shared convex optimization problem. Its setting is homogeneous: every machine can estimate gradients of the same population objective, so the analysis concerns workers pursuing a common underlying target.

The proposed stochastic Newton algorithm also uses information about curvature through stochastic Hessian-vector products. These products apply an independent, unbiased estimate of the objective's Hessian to a chosen vector. They give the algorithm access to second-order information alongside ordinary gradient estimates. Each machine can perform many such stochastic computations between communication rounds, allowing more local computation to support less frequent coordination.

The authors prove convergence guarantees for quasi-self-concordant objectives, a class that includes logistic regression, and provide empirical evidence. Within this setting, their method can reduce both the number and frequency of communication rounds without sacrificing performance relative to existing methods. The contribution connects access to stochastic curvature information with a concrete reduction in distributed communication requirements.
neurips-2021-a-stochastic-newton-algorit.tldr: A stochastic Newton method uses local gradient and curvature computations to reduce communication in homogeneous distributed convex optimization.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether visual Transformers are more robust than convolutional neural networks, or whether earlier comparisons gave them advantages through experimental design. The authors identify differences in model scale and training frameworks in prior comparisons. They then use a unified training setup to investigate which robustness differences remain when those factors are better controlled.

For adversarial robustness, the findings challenge the view that Transformers necessarily have the advantage. CNNs can match their resistance to adversarial attacks when they adopt suitable Transformer training recipes. This makes the training procedure a central part of interpreting robustness results: an observed difference between models does not by itself establish that their architectures caused it.

The picture differs for generalization to samples outside the training distribution. The authors show that Transformers can outperform CNNs without pretraining on external large-scale datasets. Their ablation studies suggest that much of this advantage comes from self-attention-like architectural features. The results therefore distinguish two kinds of robustness and give different explanations for the advantages observed in each.
neurips-2021-are-transformers-more-robus.tldr: Controlled comparisons show that training recipes can close adversarial robustness gaps, while self-attention-like architectures appear to help out-of-distribution generalization.

paragraphs: Evaluating an adversarial defense requires attacks capable of exposing its particular weaknesses. A defense can appear effective when the chosen attacks fail to exploit how it works. Existing evaluation approaches depend either on experts crafting attacks for individual defenses or on collections of fixed attacks, whose members may all be poorly suited to a particular model.

The paper proposes automating the discovery of adaptive attacks. Its central observation is that such attacks can be assembled from reusable components. By representing those components and their combinations as a search space, the method can look for attacks suited to an unfamiliar defense. This turns part of the expert's design task into a search problem.

The authors evaluate the approach on 24 defenses and report stronger results than AutoAttack. For 10 models, their tool produces 3.0%–50.8% additional adversarial examples; for the remaining models, attacks are slightly stronger or similar. These findings show that searching over adaptable attack components can reveal weaknesses missed by a strong fixed evaluation tool in the tested defenses.
neurips-2021-automated-discovery-of-adap.tldr: Searching combinations of reusable attack components exposes weaknesses that fixed adversarial evaluation attacks can miss.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions whose consequences change future rewards. In its bandit setting, an action does more than produce an immediate payoff: the history of chosen actions influences what later choices can yield. The lending example illustrates the concern, since repeated rejection of a group can affect its future ability to repay and reinforce disadvantage.

The authors formulate a stochastic multi-armed bandit model that explicitly includes this dependence on action history. The learner seeks to maximize utility over time while accounting for the dynamics its own decisions create. This changes the learning problem because the rewards available in the future depend partly on the policy followed in the past.

The proposed algorithm has regret bounded by roughly K times T to the two-thirds power, up to logarithmic factors, where K counts arms and T is the horizon. A lower bound matches that dependence without the hidden logarithmic factors. Together, the bounds characterize the difficulty of the formulated problem and provide techniques relevant to decision systems with long-term effects, including questions of fairness.
neurips-2021-bandit-learning-with-delaye.tldr: A bandit model captures how past actions alter future rewards and admits an algorithm with regret matching a lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems can receive several kinds of feedback, including clicks, missing clicks, and dislikes. These signals have complex relationships with the intentions behind a user's behavior. The paper studies how to learn representations that separate those intentions while handling noise in both input features and feedback labels. Methods focused only on positive feedback leave these additional relationships and noise sources unaddressed.

The proposed Curriculum Disentangled Recommendation model combines two mechanisms. A co-filtering dynamic routing mechanism learns relationships among feedback types and user intentions while removing noise from feature representations. An adjustable, self-evaluating curriculum estimates the difficulty of training examples and disregards useless information at the label level. The two components therefore address different places where noise enters learning.

Experiments on several real-world datasets show significant recommendation-accuracy improvements over several state-of-the-art methods. The findings support treating varied feedback as structured evidence about user intentions while also filtering unreliable information. Although separating intentions motivates potential explainability benefits, the stated experimental finding concerns improved recommendation accuracy.
neurips-2021-curriculum-disentangled-rec.tldr: CDR learns separate user intentions from varied feedback by combining feature denoising with a curriculum that filters noisy labels.

paragraphs: MetaHG addresses the detection of illicit drug traffickers on Instagram by combining the content of social-media activity with relationships among entities. The paper identifies two challenges: post content alone provides an incomplete view of the activity, and training a detection model can require substantial data. Its framework brings graph representation learning and meta-learning together to address these issues.

The method first builds a heterogeneous graph representing different kinds of entities and relationships in the trafficking ecosystem. A relation-based graph convolutional network learns user representations from this graph. Because connections among entities can be sparse, a graph refinement component modifies the structure to support more robust representation learning.

Meta-learning is then used to optimize the model, while self-supervision and knowledge distillation help exploit unlabeled data. This lets the framework draw information from content, relational structure, and examples without labels. Experiments on real-world Instagram data show that MetaHG outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The reported result supports the combined framework for the studied detection task, with its multiple components addressing complementary sources of information and training difficulty.
neurips-2021-distilling-meta-knowledge-o.tldr: MetaHG combines heterogeneous graphs, meta-learning, and unlabeled-data learning to improve illicit drug trafficker detection on Instagram.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search needs to consider the hardware on which a model will run. A model's latency is device-specific, so collecting enough measurements to build a separate predictor for every platform can become expensive. This paper addresses the measurement burden by learning a latency predictor that can adapt to an unseen device using only a few observations.

The proposed Hardware-adaptive Efficient Latency Predictor, or HELP, frames this adaptation as a meta-learning problem. It represents hardware through embeddings based on observed latency behavior, treating a device as a black box that returns execution times. These embeddings condition the predictor, allowing its estimates to depend on the target hardware rather than assuming a single relationship between architecture and speed.

On unseen platforms, HELP achieves strong latency estimation with as few as 10 measurements and outperforms the relevant baselines evaluated. The authors also incorporate it into complete architecture-search workflows. Under latency constraints, those workflows substantially reduce the total time required by the underlying search method. The findings connect efficient device adaptation to savings in the broader model-design process.
neurips-2021-hardware-adaptive-efficient.tldr: HELP uses meta-learning and hardware embeddings to predict latency on unseen devices from as few as 10 measurements.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement learning often stores past experiences and revisits them during training. This improves sample efficiency, but retaining images and repeatedly processing them with convolutional networks requires considerable memory and computation. Stored Embeddings for Efficient Reinforcement Learning, or SEER, modifies existing off-policy methods to reduce both costs.

The approach freezes the lower layers of the visual encoder early in training, motivated by the early convergence of their parameters. Once these layers are frozen, their gradient updates no longer need to be computed. SEER also stores compact latent vectors for experience replay instead of high-dimensional images. This reduces the memory required per stored experience and enables the replay buffer's capacity to increase adaptively under a memory budget.

Across the tested DeepMind Control environments and Atari games, SEER saves substantial computation and memory without degrading agent performance. The result matters because it addresses the cost of reusing experience, alongside the amount of experience needed. Its two changes connect the stabilization of visual features during learning with a more economical way to store and train on past observations.
neurips-2021-improving-computational-eff.tldr: SEER freezes early visual-encoder layers and replays compact embeddings to save computation and memory without degrading performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Saliency methods try to explain a prediction by highlighting the input features that matter to a neural network. Many derive those explanations from gradients, so noisy gradients can lead to misleading feature attributions. This paper tackles that problem during training by encouraging the network to rely less on features associated with small, potentially noisy gradients.

The training procedure repeatedly masks those features and compares the model's outputs on masked and original inputs. It trains the network to make these outputs similar. In effect, predictions are encouraged to remain stable when the selected low-gradient features disappear. The procedure aims to reduce noisy gradient information while preserving the model's ability to perform its prediction task.

The authors evaluate the method on synthetic and real datasets spanning vision, language, and time series, using recurrent networks, convolutional networks, and Transformers. Both qualitative and quantitative evaluations show significant interpretability improvements while retaining predictive performance. These results support the idea that the usefulness of saliency explanations can be improved by changing model training, alongside the methods used to produce explanations.
neurips-2021-improving-deep-learning-int.tldr: Saliency-guided training improves interpretability by making predictions stable when features with small, potentially noisy gradients are masked.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether two neural-network agents can develop useful, understandable communication while learning a visual task from scratch. The agents are trained through unsupervised emergent communication to identify referents: their interaction must convey which object is being referred to. The task provides a setting in which communication develops through the agents' shared objective.

The resulting communication protocol is largely interpretable, and the agents can use it successfully for object types absent from training. This is a meaningful test of the learned protocol because successful interaction extends beyond the object categories encountered while it developed. The finding offers evidence that emergent communication can support this kind of generalization in the studied scenario.

Training also produces visual representations that can be reused as generic features. Their quality is comparable to that of a recent self-supervised learning model. The communication task therefore yields a second useful outcome alongside the protocol itself: a reusable visual representation. Together, these findings connect learning to communicate with learning visual features and demonstrate their compatibility in a more realistic referent-identification setting.
neurips-2021-interpretable-agent-communi.tldr: Two visual agents learn a largely interpretable communication protocol that transfers to unseen object types and produces reusable visual features.

paragraphs: Counterfactual reasoning asks what would have happened under a different action or treatment. In a structural causal model, answering such questions requires mechanisms that turn noise into outcomes through deterministic functions. The paper starts from a fundamental ambiguity: observational and intervention data do not uniquely identify these mechanisms, leaving a choice even after the relevant distributions are known.

Earlier Gumbel-max mechanisms were motivated by an appealing stability property of their counterfactual predictions. This paper proposes choosing mechanisms according to quantitative objectives, such as reducing the variance of estimated counterfactual treatment effects. The authors introduce a parameterized family that generalizes Gumbel-max and can be trained against losses defined over a distribution of queries.

The learned mechanisms produce lower-variance treatment-effect estimates than fixed alternatives and also generalize to queries absent from training. The contribution is a way to make the unresolved mechanism choice serve an explicit estimation objective. It does not eliminate the stated identification ambiguity; instead, it uses that flexibility to improve performance on counterfactual questions of interest.
neurips-2021-learning-generalized-gumbel.tldr: Learnable generalizations of Gumbel-max mechanisms use explicit objectives to reduce variance in counterfactual treatment-effect estimation.

paragraphs: Many networks contain connections with a direction, including citations, website links, and traffic flows. That direction carries information that an undirected graph representation does not explicitly preserve. MagNet is a graph neural network designed to incorporate both connection structure and direction through a mathematical representation called the magnetic Laplacian.

This representation is a complex Hermitian matrix. The magnitudes of its entries encode the underlying undirected geometry, while their phases encode directional information. A charge parameter adjusts how its spectral information responds to differences among directed cycles. This gives the network a structured way to represent direction together with graph geometry within the same underlying matrix.

The authors evaluate MagNet on directed-graph node classification and link prediction. It performs well across the tested tasks and exceeds all compared methods on a majority of them. These results support the usefulness of the magnetic-Laplacian representation for the evaluated directed networks. The authors also state that its underlying principles can be adapted to other graph neural network architectures, extending the design idea beyond this particular network.
neurips-2021-magnet-a-neural-network-for.tldr: MagNet encodes graph geometry and edge direction in a magnetic Laplacian to support learning on directed networks.

paragraphs: Predicting video frames requires understanding how visual content moves across time. This paper introduces a Motion-Aware Unit, or MAU, that gives predictive units access to a broader temporal context. Its goal is to recover more reliable motion information by drawing on historical states rather than limiting the temporal information available to the prediction unit.

MAU combines attention and fusion modules. Attention compares the current spatial state with historical spatial states, then uses those correlations to aggregate historical temporal states into augmented motion information. The fusion module combines this motion information with the current appearance representation to predict a frame. An additional information-recalling scheme in the encoder and decoder helps preserve visual detail.

The authors describe MAU as relatively inexpensive computationally and easy to incorporate into other predictive models. Experiments cover both video prediction and early action recognition, with reported improvements over state-of-the-art methods on both tasks. These findings support the usefulness of selecting and combining a wider history of motion information, both for generating future frames and for recognizing actions from their early progression.
neurips-2021-mau-a-motion-aware-unit-for.tldr: MAU uses attention over historical states to enrich motion information and improve video prediction and early action recognition.

paragraphs: Density estimation aims to recover a probability distribution's shape from samples. This paper considers the problem when the estimator receives only a limited number of bits about each sample. The restriction makes communication part of the statistical problem: useful information must fit into a small message before it can contribute to the final estimate.

For densities in Besov spaces, the authors construct an adaptive, noninteractive estimator using sparse wavelet representations. They combine this with a simulate-and-infer technique drawn from communication-constrained parametric estimation. To assess its performance, they derive minimax lower bounds, which describe unavoidable estimation difficulty. Those bounds apply even to interactive protocols, giving a stronger comparison than restricting every competitor to noninteractive communication.

The resulting estimator is nearly rate-optimal, showing that its accuracy approaches these fundamental limits. It is also almost rate-optimal for Sobolev spaces. The authors leave open whether the Fourier basis, a natural representation for that class, can achieve equivalent performance. This distinction highlights that a representation well suited to an ordinary estimation problem may still require separate analysis under communication limits.
neurips-2021-optimal-rates-for-nonparame.tldr: A noninteractive wavelet estimator approaches optimal density-estimation rates when each sample can communicate only a limited number of bits.

paragraphs: Lidar data arrives as a stream, making it possible to process wedge-shaped sectors before a complete scan is available. This can reduce perception latency, but representing those sectors as Cartesian rectangles wastes memory and computation. PolarStream uses polar coordinates to better match the geometry of the arriving data for object detection and segmentation.

The method also addresses the limited spatial context of processing one sector at a time. It adds multi-scale padding using neighboring sectors: the preceding sector from the current scan, the following sector from an earlier scan, or both. Its polar convolutional architecture further incorporates feature undistortion and range-stratified convolutions. These changes refine how the system processes features within the polar representation.

Experiments on nuScenes show significant improvements over other streaming methods. PolarStream also achieves results comparable to existing methods that process full scans, while operating at lower latency. The findings show how matching the representation to the sensor's streaming geometry, together with borrowing neighboring context, can make partial-scan perception more effective without giving up its latency advantage.
neurips-2021-polarstream-streaming-objec.tldr: PolarStream combines polar-coordinate lidar sectors with neighboring context to improve streaming perception while maintaining low latency.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovering a low-rank matrix when some measurements contain large corruptions and the true rank is unknown. The method represents the matrix through factors whose chosen rank may exceed the true rank. It combines this oversized representation with an absolute-error loss and optimizes the resulting nonconvex, nonsmooth problem using subgradients with decreasing step sizes.

The authors prove exact recovery under a condition called the restricted direction preserving property, which constrains the sensing matrices and corruption. With an oversized factor rank, convergence is sublinear; when the factor rank matches the true rank, the guarantee improves to a linear rate. They also establish the condition in settings involving Gaussian measurements and independent or adversarial sparse corruption.

Numerical experiments verify exact recovery and the stated convergence behavior in the oversized setting. Further experiments indicate that the particular decreasing-step-size design can prevent overfitting in overparameterized robust recovery models, including robust matrix sensing and deep image priors. The paper presents that regularizing effect as a promising observation requiring further investigation, alongside its conditional recovery theory.
neurips-2021-rank-overspecified-robust-m.tldr: Under a stated regularity condition, a diminishing-step-size subgradient method exactly recovers corrupted low-rank matrices even when the factor rank is oversized.

paragraphs: A penalty on network weights also influences which predictors are inexpensive for the network to represent. This paper studies that relationship for linear neural networks, where the mapping from parameters to a linear predictor depends on the architecture. Its central object is representation cost: the regularization cost in predictor space induced by an l2 penalty on the underlying weights.

The authors identify these costs for certain sparse linear convolutional networks and residual networks. This analysis separates the form of the weight penalty from its effect on the represented predictor. Even when training uses the same simple l2 regularization, different parameterizations can translate that penalty into different preferences over linear predictors.

The paper also reverses the question by asking which desired predictor-space regularizers can arise through a suitable parameterization. It considers examples including lp norms, group norms, the k-support norm, and elastic net, and designs parameterizations that induce such costs. This turns representation-cost analysis into a design tool: architecture can be chosen partly for the regularization effect it creates under a simple weight penalty.
neurips-2021-representation-costs-of-lin.tldr: The paper characterizes how linear-network parameterizations turn l2 weight penalties into predictor regularizers and designs parameterizations for desired costs.

paragraphs: Community detection groups network nodes into relatively well-connected communities. Much of its statistical theory concerns networks considered as a complete object, while practical networks can grow as new nodes arrive. This paper studies the resulting computational constraint: after each arrival, a detection algorithm should perform only a limited number of updates.

The authors introduce a streaming stochastic block model to formalize network growth. Within this model, they examine voting approaches, which meet the update constraint but may not use the available network information effectively. They prove fundamental limitations for these algorithms, establishing that computationally convenient local decisions can leave useful information unexploited in the modeled setting.

The proposed alternative is STREAMBP, a streaming belief-propagation method. The paper proves its optimality in certain regimes and validates the theoretical findings using synthetic and real data. The qualified optimality result matters because it identifies settings where a streaming method can reach the relevant statistical limit while respecting incremental processing. The work connects community-detection accuracy with the practical requirement to update a growing network efficiently.
neurips-2021-streaming-belief-propagatio.tldr: STREAMBP performs incremental community detection and is provably optimal in certain regimes where voting methods face fundamental limitations.

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning asks an agent to reach different requested goals, including goals that require long sequences of actions. Existing combinations of policies and graph planning can struggle in large, high-dimensional environments and depend on a separate mechanism for gathering exploratory experience. Successor Feature Landmarks, or SFL, addresses exploration and goal-directed behavior within one framework.

SFL uses successor features to capture transition dynamics. Those features help estimate how novel a state is, guiding exploration, and support a landmark graph that provides a higher-level representation for planning. The same features directly determine a goal-conditioned policy for traveling between landmarks. Plans toward frontier landmarks then take the agent to the edge of the area it has explored.

Experiments in MiniGrid and ViZDoom show efficient exploration of large, high-dimensional state spaces and better performance than state-of-the-art baselines on long-horizon goal-conditioned tasks. The approach matters because its representation supports three connected needs: deciding where to explore, planning through known territory, and executing movement between landmarks. Exploration consequently feeds the structure used for reaching later goals.
neurips-2021-successor-feature-landmarks.tldr: SFL uses successor features for novelty-driven exploration, landmark planning, and travel between landmarks to improve long-horizon goal-reaching.

paragraphs: SurvITE studies how treatment effects vary across individuals when the outcome is the time until an event. This combines treatment-effect estimation with survival analysis. The paper focuses on discrete-time, treatment-specific conditional hazard functions, which describe event risk at a given time conditional on survival so far and the relevant individual information.

The authors identify several covariate-shift challenges in this setting that go beyond simply combining familiar confounding and censoring biases. They analyze these shifts by adapting generalization bounds from domain adaptation and treatment-effect estimation. This theoretical analysis informs the design of a deep learning method that balances learned representations for treatment-specific hazard estimation.

Across a range of experimental settings, the resulting method outperforms baselines by addressing covariate shifts from multiple sources. The significance is that estimating treatment effects over time requires attention to how the populations relevant to learning and prediction differ. The framework targets hazard estimation as a route toward understanding treatment effects on instantaneous risk and survival probabilities, bringing those distributional differences into both the analysis and model design.
neurips-2021-survite-learning-heterogene.tldr: SurvITE uses balanced representations to address multiple covariate shifts when estimating treatment-specific risks from time-to-event data.

paragraphs: The paper studies a teaching interaction in which a learner proposes a hypothesis and asks whether it is correct. A teacher either confirms it or provides a counterexample showing where it fails. Earlier work extensively considered random or worst-case counterexamples. Here, the teacher deliberately chooses the most helpful available counterexamples for teaching a target hypothesis.

The authors introduce LwEQ-TD, a teaching-dimension measure for this equivalence-query setting. It captures teaching complexity through the number of queries needed when counterexamples are selected by an optimal teacher. This makes the teacher's ability to choose informative corrections an explicit part of the mathematical problem, rather than treating every valid counterexample as equally useful.

For different hypothesis classes, the paper shows that best-case counterexamples can substantially reduce query requirements compared with random or worst-case responses. It also establishes connections with existing teaching-dimension notions for learning from samples. These results clarify how purposeful feedback can change learning complexity and relate an interactive teaching process to more familiar settings where the teacher supplies examples directly.
neurips-2021-teaching-via-best-case-coun.tldr: An optimal teacher can substantially reduce equivalence queries by selecting helpful counterexamples, formalized through a new teaching-dimension measure.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling needs a way to turn its sampled reward estimates into an action. In combinatorial bandits, earlier analyses assumed an exact optimization oracle that always finds an optimal solution. That requirement can be impractical when the underlying optimization problem is computationally hard. The paper asks what happens when Thompson sampling instead uses a common greedy approximation oracle.

The authors derive a problem-dependent regret lower bound proportional to log T divided by the square of a reward gap, where T is the time horizon. They also establish an almost matching upper bound. Together, these results quantify the learning difficulty associated with the greedy oracle and show how that difficulty depends on both elapsed time and reward separation.

An earlier failure example involved a specially constructed approximation oracle, leaving uncertainty about more common alternatives. This paper supplies theoretical results for a widely used greedy oracle and shows that approximation does not automatically prevent Thompson sampling from working. Its contribution is specific to the analyzed setting: it establishes a meaningful positive result while also identifying the regret cost that the learner can face.
neurips-2021-the-hardness-analysis-of-th.tldr: Almost matching regret bounds show that Thompson sampling can work with a greedy approximation oracle while quantifying its learning difficulty.

paragraphs: This paper identifies a structural condition under which a neural network can learn complex features by building on simpler ones. The condition, called the staircase property, applies to functions on the Boolean hypercube. It requires higher-order Fourier coefficients to be reachable through increasing chains from lower-order coefficients, providing a mathematical route from simpler interactions to more complex ones.

For functions satisfying this property, the authors prove polynomial-time learnability using layerwise stochastic coordinate descent on regular neural networks. These networks have specified homogeneity properties in their architectures and initializations. The analysis shows the learning algorithm greedily combining lower-level features into higher-level features as it progresses through network depth.

Experiments further show staircase functions being learned by more standard ResNet architectures trained with stochastic gradient descent. These empirical findings complement the theorem without replacing its particular conditions. The contribution gives a sufficient structural explanation for hierarchical learning: when the target's interactions form suitable chains, gradient-based learning can build them progressively. It connects properties of the target function with an explicit mechanism for learning across layers.
neurips-2021-the-staircase-property-how-.tldr: The staircase property supplies a sufficient structure for efficient hierarchical learning, with a theorem for regular networks and supporting ResNet experiments.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces outputs with interacting parts, making the size of the possible label set an important concern in generalization analysis. This paper derives sharper bounds on how well learned predictors transfer beyond their training data. It uses factor-graph decompositions to analyze structured prediction algorithms and develops margin guarantees under three different kinds of conditions.

Under Lipschitz continuity, the bounds improve dependence on label-set size from a square root to a logarithm. Under smoothness, the authors retain logarithmic label dependence while obtaining a convergence rate of order 1/n in the sample size n. Under a condition on space capacity, the bounds remove label-set-size dependence and converge faster than the usual 1/square-root-of-n rate.

These are separate conditional guarantees, so their benefits depend on which assumptions apply to a particular learning problem. The paper supplies applications in each case suggesting that the relevant conditions can be readily satisfied. The results sharpen the theoretical account of structured prediction by showing how properties of the learning setup can substantially reduce the apparent cost of large output spaces.
neurips-2021-towards-sharper-generalizat.tldr: New conditional generalization bounds reduce or eliminate label-set-size dependence and, in some settings, improve sample-size convergence rates.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled data alongside labeled examples, but the two collections may differ in both the classes they contain and their feature distributions. This paper studies that combined mismatch under the name Universal Semi-Supervised Learning. Its setting broadens approaches that consider only a particular class mismatch while leaving feature-domain differences unaddressed.

The proposed CAFA framework first scores unlabeled examples to identify data belonging to classes shared with the labeled collection. It then applies domain adaptation to the detected examples so they can contribute more effectively to semi-supervised consistency training. The framework requires no prior knowledge of the relationship between the two datasets' class sets.

Experiments across several benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness on open-set problems. The approach matters because deciding which unlabeled examples are relevant and accounting for how they differ from labeled data are connected challenges. Detecting shared classes addresses relevance, while adapting their feature distributions helps the training procedure use those examples. CAFA combines both operations within one framework for the more general mismatch setting.
neurips-2021-universal-semi-supervised-l.tldr: CAFA identifies shared-class unlabeled data and adapts its features to support semi-supervised learning when both classes and domains differ.
